title: But what is a neural network? (3Blue1Brown)
summary: The video introduces the structure of a plain vanilla neural network, using the classic task of recognizing handwritten digits from 28x28 pixel images as its running example. It explains neurons as things holding activations between 0 and 1, organized into an input layer of 784 pixels, two hidden layers and an output layer of 10 digits. It then motivates the layered structure as a hope that hidden layers detect edges and then patterns like loops and lines, before showing how weights, biases and the sigmoid function determine each layer's activations from the previous one. Finally it expresses this compactly as a matrix-vector product, frames the whole network as a function with about 13,000 parameters, and closes with a discussion of why modern networks often use ReLU instead of sigmoid.

topics.name: Neurons, layers and activations
topics.summary: Starting from the difficulty of recognizing handwritten digits by program, it introduces neurons as holders of activations between 0 and 1, arranged in an input layer of 784 pixels, hidden layers and a 10-neuron output layer whose brightest neuron is the network's answer.

topics.name: Why layered structure helps
topics.summary: Explains the hope that hidden layers build layers of abstraction, with early neurons detecting small edges and later ones detecting loops and lines that combine into digits, an idea that extends to tasks like speech parsing.

topics.name: Weights, biases and sigmoid
topics.summary: Shows how a neuron's activation is computed as a weighted sum of the previous layer's activations plus a bias, squished into the range 0 to 1 by the sigmoid function, and how these roughly 13,000 parameters are what learning must set.

topics.name: Matrix notation for layers
topics.summary: Rewrites the transition between layers compactly as a weight matrix times an activation vector plus a bias vector, passed through sigmoid element-wise, and reframes the entire network as one complicated function from 784 inputs to 10 outputs.

topics.name: ReLU versus sigmoid
topics.summary: A closing discussion explains that modern deep networks rarely use sigmoid and instead use the rectified linear unit, max(0, a), because it is much easier to train.
